options.text: Round-trip network latency, by sending many commands without waiting for each reply

questions.explanation: Pipelining amortizes round-trip time: you send a batch of commands back-to-back and read all the replies together, paying the RTT roughly once instead of once per command.

questions.prompt: Does pipelining make the batched commands atomic?

options.text: No — it only removes waiting; other clients' commands can still interleave

questions.explanation: Pipelining is purely a latency optimization with no atomicity. For atomic execution you need MULTI/EXEC or a Lua script.

questions.prompt: Which are O(N) traps that can block the single command thread? Select all that apply.

options.text: HGETALL on a hash with millions of fields
LRANGE key 0 -1 on a huge list
GET on a single small string

questions.explanation: KEYS, big HGETALL, and full LRANGE are all O(N) and stall the server. A single GET is O(1) and fine.

questions.prompt: In Redis 6+, what do I/O threads speed up?

options.text: The execution of each command's logic
Reading and writing data on the network sockets (not command execution)

questions.explanation: I/O threads parallelize moving bytes on the network; command execution stays single-threaded, so they won't speed up an expensive command.

questions.prompt: The command that lists recent commands which exceeded a time threshold is ______. (one word)
questions.explanation: SLOWLOG records commands slower than slowlog-log-slower-than microseconds; SLOWLOG GET shows them.

questions.prompt: What should you use instead of DEL to remove a very large key without blocking?

options.text: UNLINK, which frees the memory in the background

questions.explanation: UNLINK removes the key immediately but reclaims its (potentially large) memory asynchronously, avoiding the blocking cost that DEL would pay freeing a huge value.
